newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia stocks rally as Fed rate hike fear fades.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks rally as Fed rate hike fear fades.

text.p: Stock markets across Asia got off to a roaring start on Monday following Wall Street's climb to record levels on the back of fresh U.S. economic data that calmed jitters over higher interest rates.
Investors swept into the markets following news of weaker-than-expected gains in both the latest U.S. consumer price index and retails sales.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 67 points to close at a record of 5,839, and bond prices rallied with the key 30-year government bond gaining nearly 1-1/2 points.
It was the first time the Dow closed above 5,800. The previous record close was 5,778 on May 24.
"It was a buying frenzy based on the weaker-than-expected consumer prices and retail sales," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
"The data clearly suggest the Fed does not need to raise interest rates at its upcoming...meeting," he added.
The policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next meets on September 24.

Global financial markets had been awash with speculation that the FOME would vote to push interest rates higher based on earlier economic figures that suggested the Fed may raise rates to make a preemptive strick against inflation.
Hong Kong stocks rose sharply, with the key Hang Seng Index approaching its 1996 high of 11,600 before easing slightly. Turnover was a heafty HK$1.1billion after only 15 minutes of trade.
"It's powering ahead," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities.
"It's only because everyone knew the market was headed up in the morning," he said of the heavy volume.
At midday, the Hang Seng was up 179.28 points, or 1.58 percent, at 11,548.32.
Tokyo stocks were closed for a public holiday. The key Nikkei 225-share average closed Friday up 398.71 points, or 1.95 percent at 20,842.64.
Philippine shares shot up nearly 40 points, or 1.25 percent, to 3,233.67 points, while stocks in Indonesia rose 6.1 points or 1.11 percent to 555.15.
"More than anything else, it was a turnaround in sentiment -- from tentative to positive," said Lito Vicencio, manager of Peregrine Securities in Manila.
Thai stocks were up 19.28 points or 1.85 percent to 1,058.93 in thin trade.

Brokers said that there was some buying by investors on expectations that local political problems may ease after an upcoming no-confidence motion against Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa is debated in parliament on September 18 and 19.
Korean shares were higher as investors concentrated on buying blue chip and large cap shares after recent declines. The composite stock index was up 3.01 points or 0.39 percent at 784.74.
Taiwan's weighted index was up 53.91 points, or 0.83 percent, at 6,518.46 at midday.
In Singapore, shares opened higher, but dealers said the focus was on Malaysian shares.
The Straits Times Index was up 16.25 points, or 0.76 percent, at 2,142.52, while in Malaysia the KLSE composite index was up 11.55 points at 1,129.10.
Australia's All Ordinaries index was up 15.60 points at 2,267.90, while New Zealand's 40-cap index was up 7.56 at 2,221.45.
Crude oil futures prices slumped in response to comments from Iraq on Friday that it would suspend air defence attacks on U.S. and allied aircraft patrolling no-fly zones.
November North Sea Brent crude traded on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) was quoted 25-65 cents below the Friday London close of US$23.13 per barrel.
